title: Pip’s Picnic Pack
tagline: Hear the word. Find what helps.
learningGoal: Use a spoken everyday word or short functional description to choose a suitable pictured object, including a changed example.
childTakeaway: Things can look different and still help us do the same job.
story: Pip is packing a picnic and needs help finding objects for a drink, soup, and a small spill.
introPip: Will you help me pack my picnic? Listen, then point to a thing that can help.
conceptImageAlt: A smiling silver-gray ball with blue seams sits beside an open picnic basket, a blue handled cup, a yellow handleless cup, a plate and bread roll, a bowl of smooth soup, a spoon, a cloth napkin, and an apple on a teal blanket in a sunny park.

ageSupport.entry: A grown-up may say the prompt in the child’s home language, name every pictured option neutrally, or demonstrate the action with real objects. Accept pointing, signing, or speech; repeat freely.
ageSupport.stretch: After a choice, invite the child to name another thing that can do that job or explain the choice. Round five is optional; accepting either sensible vessel is enough.

misconception: An object’s color, handle, or familiar appearance is not its whole meaning. A cup can look different, and more than one object can do the same job.

rounds.title: A drink for Pip
rounds.prompt: Pip is thirsty. Which thing helps Pip drink water?
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip and a water droplet above two equally sized choice panels: a blue handled cup on the left and a shallow white plate on the right.
rounds.success: The cup holds a drink. Pip can lift it and take a sip.
hints: Look for a place to hold Pip’s drink.
Pretend to lift each thing and take a sip. Which is made to hold a drink?
This is a cup. Water stays inside its deep sides, ready for a sip.
rounds.visualHint: After help is requested, show water going into the cup and a simple tipping-for-a-sip demonstration; show the plate’s shallow surface without declaring all plates incapable of holding any liquid.
rounds.whyThisRound: Starts with a familiar functional association and two distinct silhouettes; no reading or naming aloud is required.

rounds.title: A cup can look different
rounds.prompt: Find a cup for Pip’s drink.
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip and a picnic basket above three equal choice panels: a shallow white plate on the left, a red apple in the middle, and a yellow handleless cup on the right.
rounds.success: This cup has no handle, and it is still a cup. Its sides hold a drink.
hints: A cup does not have to be blue.
Look at the open top and deep sides. Try imagining a drink inside.
The yellow one is a cup too. Cups can have different colors and shapes, with or without a handle.
rounds.visualHint: On request, place the earlier blue cup beside the new yellow cup outside the choice area; trace the opening and deep sides on both, then fill them equally.
rounds.whyThisRound: Changes color, shape, handle, and position so a remembered blue-cup picture is insufficient.

rounds.title: Scoop smooth soup
rounds.prompt: Pip has smooth soup. Which tool can scoop it?
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip and a bowl of smooth orange soup above two equal choice panels: a silver fork on the left and a silver spoon on the right.
rounds.success: The spoon’s little bowl can scoop the smooth soup. A fork’s gaps let it run through.
hints: Think about lifting some smooth soup.
Look closely at the end of each tool. One has a little bowl; one has gaps.
The spoon can hold a scoop of smooth soup in its little bowl. Choose the spoon.
rounds.visualHint: Only after requesting help, animate each listed tool dipping into the same smooth soup: a spoon lifts liquid while liquid passes between the fork’s tines. Do not use chunky soup or imply that people must use spoons to eat all soup.
rounds.whyThisRound: A closer comparison between two eating tools checks function rather than broad picnic membership.

rounds.title: Clean a little spill
rounds.prompt: Pip spilled water. Choose one thing that can wipe it up.
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip and a small blue water puddle above three equal panels: a sponge on the left, a folded cloth napkin in the middle, and a silver fork on the right.
rounds.success: A sponge or a cloth can wipe up this little spill. You found a thing that helps.
hints: Look for something that can soak up a little water.
Imagine pressing the sponge or cloth onto the spill. They can take up water.
The sponge and the cloth can both help. Choose either one.
rounds.visualHint: After help, show both the sponge and cloth in separate equal demonstrations absorbing a portion of a small water spill; neither should be treated as the only approved household method.
rounds.whyThisRound: Transfers from naming containers and tools to an action word, and explicitly accepts two appropriate objects.

rounds.title: More than one way
rounds.prompt: Choose one thing that can hold water for drinking.
rounds.sceneAlt: Pip and a water droplet above three equal panels: a blue handled cup on the left, a silver fork in the middle, and a deep teal bowl on the right.
rounds.success: The cup and the bowl can both hold water. People can drink from different kinds of vessels.
hints: Look for an open inside with sides around it.
Imagine pouring a little water into the cup and the bowl. Where can it stay?
The cup and the bowl can both hold a drink. Choose either one.
rounds.visualHint: On help request, add an equal water level to the cup and bowl. Show sipping from each as optional examples, with no hierarchy between the two.
rounds.whyThisRound: Optional stretch separates the functional category from the word cup and welcomes familiar drinking practices from different households.

finale: Pip has a drink, a tool for the soup, and something to clean the spill. The basket opens onto a calm picnic; Pip uses the chosen suitable objects.
offlineActivity: With a grown-up, put out a cup, a bowl, a spoon, a fork, and a small cloth. Ask, 'What could help us have a drink?' and 'What could wipe up a little spill?' Accept a child’s sensible explanation; use a small amount of cool water only if wanted.
reviewQuestions: Should the lesson mainly practice object names, or functional language such as drink, scoop, and wipe? The current version mixes both; which emphasis fits the Gems lesson’s scope?
Do you want both sensible answers visible in rounds four and five, with any single choice accepted, or would a simpler first release use only one suitable option per question?
Are these vessels and picnic objects familiar to the intended children, and which home-language words or household alternatives should the review include?
designNotes: The generated picture introduces the story. The five deterministic SVGs are the exact question scenes and contain no instructional text.
Prompts are proposed spoken copy. This review pack has no voice files, scoring, maze, game wiring, or child-testing results.
Round three asks about a tool for smooth liquid soup; a bowl can also be lifted to drink soup. It is intentionally not a test of universal eating etiquette.
Multiple correct IDs mean any one listed choice is acceptable, not a hidden multi-select task. Round five avoids excluding drinking from a bowl.

A child who identifies an unusual sensible use should receive adult acknowledgment rather than a punitive failure. Picture recognition and English familiarity must not be mistaken for total vocabulary knowledge.
A future child interface should allow replay, home-language narration, pointing or large taps, and generous time. This adult review pack does not establish developmental validation.
Keep contrastive comparisons about object functions; do not make color matching or basket membership the answer.
Hints are proposed demonstrations, described here for review; the unassisted SVGs do not include answer-revealing arrows or highlight a correct option.
